segments.text: Spin a globe, and Earth looks like it's {m:melt}melting.
{m:sam}South America. {m:afr}Africa. {m:ind}India.
{m:grl}Greenland. {m:fla}Florida. {m:baja}Baja. {m:kam}Kamchatka.
Every point aims {m:south}south. Like somebody left the planet on the dashboard in {m:july}July.
{m:twothirds}Two-thirds of all land is north of the {m:eq}equator. So are nearly {m:nine}nine in ten of us.
You've probably heard those southern points are just a {m:coin}coincidence.
They're {m:not}not. Not {m:entirely}entirely.
So {m:why}why do the continents point south? By the end, you'll know what they're really {m:pointing}pointing at.
Along the way: why you can't dig to China from {m:usa}anywhere in America.
A theory from {m:t1875}eighteen seventy-five that explained all of it, and was {m:wrong}dead wrong. And {m:last}the last one: the four continents your country might {m:crash}crash into. Eventually.
Bad news: you're not the first to notice. {m:bacon}Not even close.
In sixteen twenty, Francis {m:fb}Bacon wrote that the Old World and the New are both {m:narrow}'narrow and pointed toward the south.'
And in the same {m:breath}breath, he said Africa and South America's matching capes were {m:accident}'not to be attributed to mere accident.'
Then he wrote down an open question: is there even a {m:southcont}southern continent down there? Nobody would lay eyes on {m:antar}Antarctica for two more {m:cent}centuries. Remember {m:rem}that.
Now, you may have heard that Bacon predicted continental drift. {m:scratch}He didn't.
He wasn't {m:snap}snapping Africa and South America together like puzzle pieces. He was saying they're shaped {m:same}alike, side by side.
So Bacon saw the drip, but never tried to {m:explain}explain it. For centuries, nobody else {m:anyone}could. That did not stop them from {m:try}trying.
Captain {m:cook}Cook's naturalist, Johann Reinhold Forster, claimed that every great southern tip looks {m:alike}alike: high, rocky, the end of a {m:mtn}mountain chain.

His {m:expl}explanation? A giant flood came {m:wave}roaring in from the south-west and {m:carved}carved every one of them. Some of the top scientists of the day {m:bought}bought it. Geology later asked for a {m:refund}refund.
By the eighteen-forties, the most famous scientist alive was calling the tips {m:pyr}'pyramidal.' And someone had written down almost the exact {m:list}list you saw at the start.
{m:l1}Greenland, {m:l2}Baja, {m:l3}Florida, {m:l4}India, {m:l5}Kamchatka. 'All their points turned towards the south.'

Then, in the {m:seventies}nineteen-seventies, the pattern got its name, as a {m:joke}joke. A magazine writer called it {m:drip}'continental drip': a fake theory you could prove just by {m:staring}staring at a map.
Three years later, a geologist published his own {m:version}version of the joke. Hold on to {m:hold}him. He matters more than you'd {m:think}think.
But the shapes are just the {m:first}first clue. The next one is on the {m:far}far side of the planet.

Start at the top of the world. The {m:np}North Pole isn't land, it's ocean. Which makes Santa's workshop, technically, a {m:boat}houseboat. Stand on the ice there, and the sea floor is about {m:depth}two and a half miles beneath your boots.
Now go to the {m:bottom}bottom. At the {m:sp}South Pole, you're standing almost {m:up}two miles up, on a {m:sheet}sheet of ice more than a mile and a half {m:thick}thick.
The two ends of the planet are {m:neg}photographic negatives. Ocean on top. A continent at the bottom.
And they're almost the same size. {m:drag}Drag the Arctic Ocean down onto Antarctica, and the sizes nearly {m:match}match.

But here's the part that doesn't make sense. They don't just match. They {m:line}line up. Most of {m:ant}Antarctica sits directly opposite the Arctic Ocean, on the exact {m:other}other side of the Earth.
And it's not just the {m:poles}poles. Almost everywhere you look, land has {m:avoid}ocean on its far side, not more land. Which {m:brings}brings us to a classic American playground {m:myth}myth.

If you dig straight down, you'll reach {m:china}China. Let's {m:test}test it. Start in {m:kansas}Kansas, right at the center of the lower forty-eight, and {m:dig}dig. Ignore everything on the way down that would kill you, and keep {m:going}going.
You come out in the {m:indian}southern Indian Ocean. The {m:nearest}nearest land is a tiny French {m:island}island, more than two hundred miles {m:away}away.
Not {m:notchina}China. Not even the right {m:hemi}hemisphere. In fact, there isn't a single spot in the {m:us}United States that sits opposite {m:china2}China.
Even if you {m:start}started in China, three times out of {m:four}four you'd surface in the ocean. The people who can actually {m:dig2}dig to China? {m:arg}Argentinians.
Now flip {m:flipall}every continent to the far side of the planet and {m:lay}lay it over the {m:orig}original. Only about {m:eighth}one-eighth of the land has land on the other side.
That's less than half of what you'd expect if the continents had been {m:random}sprinkled at random.
So try a {m:puzzle}puzzle. Slice the Earth into {m:half}two halves, any way you like, and {m:cram}cram as much land as you can into one of them.
The winner is centered on {m:europe}western Europe. It scoops up most of the world's land. And it's still {m:still}more than half water.
There is no way to {m:cut}cut this planet in half and get a half that's {m:mostly}mostly land.
Now flip the globe {m:flip}over. The other half is {m:p89}eighty-nine percent water, centered in the empty Pacific near New Zealand.
The Pacific {m:alone}alone could swallow {m:drop}every continent on Earth, with room to spare. Yes, even {m:asia}Asia.
{m:ocean}Ocean on top, {m:landb}land at the bottom, {m:avoidl}land avoiding land. This planet is strangely {m:lop}lopsided. And the drip might be just the part you can {m:see}see.
And back in {m:g1875}eighteen seventy-five, one man thought he'd found a single {m:shape}shape that explained all of it. And it wasn't a {m:ball}ball.
Before we meet him: every Myth Juice video takes {m:taught}one thing you were taught about the world and {m:checks}checks it against the real planet. Want the next one? {m:sub}Subscribe.
His name was William Lowthian Green. He wasn't a professor. He was the {m:hawaii}foreign minister of the Kingdom of Hawaii.
And he'd been {m:obsessed}obsessed with those pointy southern tips for years. He even demonstrated them with a {m:card}bent card dipped in {m:water}water.

Remember those {m:pyr2}'pyramidal' tips? Green thought the whole planet was heading that way: {m:cool}cooling, shrinking, and slowly collapsing toward a {m:tet}tetrahedron. A four-cornered {m:pyr4}pyramid.
It sounds ridiculous. But watch what it {m:pred}explained. Most land in the north: {m:c1}check. Three continents ending in points aimed south: {m:c2}check.
An ocean on top of the world: {m:c3}check. A continent at the bottom: {m:c4}check. Land sitting opposite water: {m:c5}check. One shape, every clue.
And it {m:main}caught on. By eighteen ninety-nine, a leading {m:geol}geologist was telling Britain's top geographers that a shrinking Earth had to {m:squeeze}squeeze toward a {m:geo}tetrahedron.
He even pointed out that most of North America sits opposite the {m:io}Indian Ocean. The same ocean you just dug into.
By nineteen eighteen, a children's {m:mag}magazine was telling kids that one day, the Earth would turn into a {m:pyramid}pyramid. Sleep {m:tight}tight, kids.
So, hang on. If it explained all that, {m:how}how do we know it's wrong?

Because the whole idea needed a cooling, shrinking Earth. And critics could {m:measure}measure the planet: a ball, slightly squashed at the poles. Not a {m:notp}pyramid. And by then, scientists had discovered {m:rad}radioactivity, quietly heating Earth from the inside.
Over the next few decades, the shrinking engine {m:stall}stalled. The pyramid vanished from geology. Green's checklist was {m:real}real. He'd just pinned the clues on the wrong {m:suspect}suspect.

The real suspect had been hiding in plain sight on every world {m:maps}map. A few people had guessed it before. It took one stubborn man to {m:say}make the case out loud. And his story ends on one of the {m:drips}drips.

Around nineteen ten, a young German weather scientist named Alfred Wegener {m:wrote}wrote to his future wife. Doesn't South America {m:fit}fit against Africa, he asked, as if they had once been {m:joined}joined?
'This is an idea I'll have to {m:pursue}pursue.'
In nineteen twelve, he stood up before a {m:meeting}meeting of geologists and told them the {m:move}continents move. Then a world {m:war}war buried his {m:book}book.

Once the world read it, the reaction was {m:brutal}brutal. One society president called it {m:rot}'utter, damned rot.' In Germany, he never landed a full {m:prof}professorship. It took a university in {m:austria}Austria to give him one.
And critics had one killer question: what could possibly {m:push}push a continent? Wegener guessed Earth's {m:spin}spin, and tides. Both were far too {m:weak}weak.
He admitted it himself. 'The Newton of drift theory has not yet {m:appeared}appeared.'
In nineteen thirty, Wegener was deep on the ice of {m:grl}Greenland. One of the drip's own tips.
On his {m:fifty}fiftieth birthday, he left a {m:camp}camp in the middle of the ice sheet with a Greenlander named Rasmus {m:villumsen}Villumsen.
Neither of them made it {m:back}back.
They found Wegener's body the next {m:may}May, carefully buried in the snow. Villumsen was never {m:found}found.

Wegener never saw his idea proven. The proof was hiding on the {m:floor}ocean floor: stripes of magnetized rock, {m:mirror}mirrored on both sides of the mid-ocean ridges, like a {m:tape}tape recording of new seafloor being made.
The paper that decoded those stripes came out {m:y33}thirty-three years after he died.
Today, satellites clock the continents moving at about the speed your {m:nail}fingernails grow. Or your {m:toe}toenails, depending on which government agency you ask.
So Wegener was {m:right}right. But that still doesn't explain the {m:drip}drip. Why would so many of them end up {m:point}pointing the same way?
Run the clock {m:rewind}backwards, and the big drips all start pointing at the same {m:place}place.
Back into the age of dinosaurs. Watch the southern continents slide home: {m:r_sam}South America, {m:r_afr}Africa, {m:r_ind}India, {m:r_aus}Australia.
They lock together into one supercontinent: {m:gond}Gondwana. And at its heart sits {m:ant}Antarctica. Geologists call it the keypiece.
{m:remember}Remember Bacon's open question? Is there even a southern continent? The drips were {m:point}pointing at it {m:whole}the whole time.
Now let the clock run {m:fwd}forward. Cracks open, and new ocean starts seeping in between {m:afant}Africa and Antarctica.

Then the {m:zip}South Atlantic unzips from the bottom up, {m:split}splitting Africa from South America. The south tears open {m:firstt}first. The last {m:seam}seam, near the equator, hangs on for millions of years {m:snap2}more.
And then everyone moves {m:leave}out. Except {m:stay}Antarctica. It barely budges. It keeps the {m:house}house.
India {m:sprint}sprints: up to about eight inches a year, several times faster than {m:afaus}Africa or Australia. For a continent, that's reckless {m:driving}driving. Then it {m:slam}slams into Asia.
Here's the {m:best}explanation a geologist will most likely give you. Put the pieces back {m:together}together, and their pointy ends all sat close to {m:ant2}Antarctica.
As they drifted {m:apart}apart, they roughly kept their orientation. So those points still {m:aim}aim back to where they tore away.
The big drips aren't drips at all. They're {m:scar}scars.
Back to that second drip joke. The geologist who wrote it was John {m:holden}Holden.
Writing for a science humor journal, he declared that every continent is a {m:tear}teardrop, with the pointed end showing the direction it came from.

Drips always flow {m:down}down, he reasoned, so our maps must be {m:upside}upside down. He was {m:joking}joking. But one of the most famous {m:photo}photos of Earth ever taken really was shot with {m:bm}Antarctica on top. It was published {m:flip}flipped.
So by Holden's logic, it was right the first {m:first}time.

And one day, he wrote, the continents would {m:splash}splash back together into a supercontinent called {m:pangooy}'Pangooy.' On a {m:tue}Tuesday, at nine in the morning. He did not say which {m:tz}time zone.
{m:twist}Here's the twist. Six years {m:earlier}earlier, the very same John Holden had helped map, for {m:real}real, how Pangaea broke {m:apart2}apart.
His joke even {m:cited}cited his own real work. That line about the {m:pointline}point showing where it came from? Not just a {m:punch}punchline. It was basically the {m:answer}answer.

And the joke wasn't {m:notdone}done. Geologists have since found {m:realdrip}real drips. Under {m:nev}Nevada, a cold blob of rock appears to be sinking into the Earth, like {m:honey}honey off a spoon. One of the scientists who found it admitted he'd been {m:anti}'anti-drip' since his early days.
Now, the honest {m:honest}part, because we're not going to fake you a tidy answer. Not everything {m:drips}drips.

Australia's {m:york}Cape York points north. So do Mexico's {m:yuc}Yucatán, Denmark's {m:jut}Jutland and Siberia's {m:tay}Taymyr. And the Antarctic {m:antpen}Peninsula has no choice. From the South Pole, every direction is {m:north}north.
Smaller drips have their own {m:stories}stories. Several million years ago, the Pacific Plate grabbed {m:baja}Baja and started dragging it away from mainland {m:mex}Mexico. It's still {m:going}going.

{m:fla}Florida isn't a drip at all. It's the top of a gigantic {m:lime}limestone platform, miles thick, built up by {m:sealife}sea life in warm, shallow water. And {m:under}under all that limestone sits bedrock that started out next to {m:wafr}West Africa. Like a lot of people in Florida, it's originally from somewhere {m:else}else.

And Africa's real southern tip isn't the Cape of Good {m:gh}Hope. It's Cape {m:agul}Agulhas. The name means {m:needles}'needles,' and the best-known story says that's because sailors' {m:compass}compass needles there pointed true north. So, if that story is right, Africa's southern tip is named after pointing {m:north2}north.

So is the drip just a {m:coin2}coincidence? The big ones are most {m:likely}likely not: they're scars from a supercontinent that tore apart around {m:v_ant}Antarctica. The small ones have no single {m:single}answer, and some of it may just be us, connecting {m:dots}dots.

And the rest of the {m:lopside}lopsided planet? The land piled up in the {m:northl}north, the land that avoids {m:avoid2}land? There's no clear sign of a deep {m:force}force arranging it. The likeliest answer: it's a {m:snap}snapshot of where the drifting pieces happen to be right now.
So where is the drip {m:going}going? Since Bacon wrote his {m:line}line, the Atlantic has grown about a {m:bus}school bus wider.

Give it a couple hundred million {m:years}years, and geologists think a new supercontinent will {m:form}form. They just can't {m:agree}agree on what it looks like. Here are the four main {m:models}models.
One: the Atlantic {m:prox}slams shut, and America {m:crash2}crashes back into Africa in about two hundred fifty million years. Pangaea {m:proxname}Proxima.
Two: the Pacific closes instead, and the Americas hit {m:novo}Antarctica first. Novopangaea. One team's favorite bet.
Three: the Arctic Ocean vanishes, and America meets {m:asia}Asia practically at the North Pole. Amasia.
Four: both oceans close at once, and Australia ends up in the {m:middle}middle of everything. Australia plus America: {m:aurica}Aurica.

{m:a1}Africa, {m:a2}Antarctica, {m:a3}Asia or {m:a4}Australia: which {m:neighbor}neighbor are you betting on? One word, in the {m:comments}comments. In a way, Holden's continental splash really is coming. Just not on a {m:tuesday}Tuesday.
One study ran the climate on one of these future supercontinents. Only a {m:tenth}tenth to a sixth of the land would stay livable for mammals. {m:mammal}Reminder: you're a mammal.
Whichever future {m:wins}wins, the map we know gets {m:torn}torn up. The drip is just a fingerprint of where the pieces have {m:been}been.

Four hundred years {m:ago}ago, Bacon said the matching capes of Africa and South America were no {m:acc2}accident. Looks like he was {m:right2}right. It wasn't an accident. It was a {m:breakup}breakup.
Every map you've ever seen is one {m:frame}frame of a very slow movie.
And the next frame is already being {m:shot}shot. Right now in {m:afar}Ethiopia, three {m:cracks}cracks meet in a giant Y, and one of them is slowly unzipping {m:eafr}East Africa.
What happens if Africa splits in two? That's our {m:here}next story. And if you want to watch the map keep changing, {m:sub2}subscribe.
